accuracy.evidence: Checked against Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, 'The spread of true and false news online' (Science 359, 2018: false stories 70% more likely to be retweeted, spread farther and faster, linked to novelty, surprise and disgust), Wineburg and McGrew, 'Lateral Reading' (Stanford History Education Group, 2017: fact-checkers leave an unfamiliar site to see what others say, while students and historians stayed on the page), Hasher, Goldstein and Toppino (1977) on the illusory truth effect, and Cancer Research UK on cold water myths. The share model is labelled as a simplified model; its numbers were recomputed (1 + s + s² + s³ + s⁴: 5, 31, 121, 341, 781). The feed shares six slots by weight with each like doubling a topic's weight, and the text describes it only as more of what you like.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented beliefs from media-literacy research: trusting a site's own About page (prediction 3, lab check 1, challenge 'about', p2), treating likes and shares as evidence (lab check 5, 'likes', m4), thinking only foolish people are fooled ('smart', m2), thinking strong feelings mean a claim is true ('feel'), rushing to share ('rush', p4), believing the feed is a neutral view of everything ('all', prediction 1, m1) and thinking a photo you took is yours alone to post ('own', p5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfeed is about how information reaches a teenager online: a six-slot feed that reallocates slots by liked-topic weight and narrows into a bubble, a share-spread model where a shock slider changes the branching and the reach ring diagram, a five-tab lateral-reading board where on-page checks turn red and off-page checks turn green, a viral post split into tappable trick segments, and a Post / Ask first / Do not post consent sort. flagnetsafe (ages 7-9) sorts private facts and kind replies; flagbias is about first impressions of people; neither models feeds, spread or lateral reading. lab_distinct gate passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees each effect before it is named: four likes leave 3 of 8 kinds of post and only then the text says filter bubble; moving the shock slider shows reach jump from 5 to 121 to 781; tapping the About page turns red with 'a site can say anything about itself' while new-tab checks turn green; plain parts of the viral post give 'plain information you could check' so the four tricks stand apart.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'the same mix as before' after four likes (the feed narrows to three kinds), 'true stories' or 'both the same' for which spreads faster (backed by the 2018 Twitter study and the shock model), and 'read its About page' as the best first check (the About tab turns red and the lateral tabs green).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with seven distinct feedback messages that name the slip: the feed is all there is, rushing to share, feelings as evidence, trusting the About page, likes as proof, only silly people are fooled, and posting others' photos without asking. Answer order rotates.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and explains each term (filter bubble, reading sideways or lateral reading) right after the example that shows it; adult text was rewritten into short sentences after the first pass read at FK 12.1 and now passes the adult limit, naming the PSHE Association KS3 programme and the key terms. Canvas labels stay short (Tricks found: 2 of 4).

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each kid paragraph covers one idea (filter bubbles, why false posts spread, checking habits, online identity and consent). Items vary the reasoning: share counts that multiply per round (p1, m3), feed counts (p3, m7), choosing a fact-checker's move (p2, m8), spotting a trick (p4), consent for photos (p5) and matching online and offline behaviour (m5).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and 360 px Android dark screenshots of every step after Show me. The first pass ran the lateral-reading tabs off the bottom of the canvas and clipped the tricks summary at 360 px, so the tabs now start higher and the summary uses short trick names at 11 px. Feed cards use two columns on phones; trick segments wrap to new lines; buttons wrap without clipping. Cards use fixed light fills with dark ink, so they read the same in both themes.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap or drag has a labelled button twin: Like Games, Like Football, Like Music and Search something new; Less shocking and More shocking; one button per check; one button per post segment; Post, Ask first and Do not post. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result (kinds of post left, reach after four rounds, what each check found, which trick was found). walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

Wineburg, S. and McGrew, S., Lateral Reading: Reading Less and Learning More When Evaluating Digital Information, Stanford History Education Group working paper (2017)
